term: Digital public infrastructure and digital public goods
oneSentence: Shared digital building blocks and reusable digital tools that help countries deliver public services, especially when they are designed for broad access and interoperability.
plainExplanation:
These terms are related, but they are not the same. Digital public infrastructure, or DPI, usually means basic digital systems that many services can rely on, such as digital identity, payments, data exchange or messaging layers. Digital public goods, or DPGs, are reusable resources in open categories, such as open-source software, open standards, open data, open AI models or open content, that also meet public-interest criteria.

A simple way to separate them is this: DPI is the service foundation, while DPGs are reusable components that may help build or improve it. A digital identity system or payment rail may be DPI. Open-source software or an open standard may qualify as a DPG used to build it. An international standard is a document agreed by a recognised standards body. It is not DPI merely because a public system uses it.

What goes in? Policy choices, funding, technical design, governance rules, security measures, and sometimes shared digital components. What happens? Organisations build or connect systems so different services can work together. Interoperability means different systems can exchange and use information in a compatible way. What comes out? Public services that can be faster, more connected and easier to scale, if they are well governed.

These terms are often discussed with AI because AI systems may sit on top of public digital systems or be distributed as reusable digital tools. But DPI and DPG do not mean AI. A country can have DPI without using AI, and not every open-source AI model is a digital public good. It must also meet the applicable DPG criteria. Those criteria should be stated because different forums may apply them differently.

everydayAnalogy.title: A town transport system and shared spare parts
everydayAnalogy.story: A town runs many bus routes, but they all depend on the same road network, bus stops, ticket readers and timetable system. Those shared basics let many routes operate together, even when different companies or districts are involved. Now imagine that several towns also share a set of well-documented ticket-reader designs and timetable software that any town can adapt without starting from zero. The first set is like digital public infrastructure; the second set is like digital public goods that can help build or improve it.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Public digital systems are not as simple as roads and bus parts. DPI involves law, rights, privacy, cybersecurity, procurement, accountability and long-term governance. Also, not every reusable digital tool qualifies as a digital public good, and a public digital system can exist even if it was not built from open components.

visual.title: How digital public goods relate to digital public infrastructure
visual.learningObjective: Show the difference between reusable digital components and the public digital systems built or operated with them.
visual.description: A two-column comparison. The left column lists reusable building blocks labelled DPGs. The right column lists public service layers labelled DPI. Arrows show that some DPGs can feed into DPI, but the columns do not fully overlap. A note at the bottom says AI may appear in either column, or neither.

steps.label: DPGs: reusable components
steps.explanation: Show examples such as open-source software, open standards, open data, open content and some open AI models. Emphasise that these are things others can reuse or adapt under defined conditions.
steps.visualInstruction: Render five stacked cards in the left column with simple icons: code brackets, ruler, database, document, network nodes. Add a small caption: 'Reusable tools and resources'.

steps.label: DPI: service foundations
steps.explanation: Show examples such as digital identity, payments, data exchange and messaging layers used across multiple public services.
steps.visualInstruction: Render four stacked cards in the right column with icons: ID card, payment symbol, linked arrows, message bubble. Add a caption: 'Shared systems used by many services'.

steps.label: How they connect
steps.explanation: Draw arrows from selected DPG cards to selected DPI cards to show that digital public goods can help build, improve or maintain digital public infrastructure.
steps.visualInstruction: Use curved arrows from 'open-source software' and 'open standards' to all four DPI cards, and from 'open data' to data exchange only. Keep arrows thin and directional.

steps.label: What they are not
steps.explanation: Add a footer note that DPI is not the same as any one app, and DPG is not the same as any open project. Governance, rights protection and fitness for public use still matter.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a full-width note box at the bottom with two short bullets and a muted warning icon.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap any card to show a one-sentence definition and one example. A toggle labelled 'Show AI examples' adds one optional card in each column to illustrate that AI can be part of either, but neither term means AI by default.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares two related ideas. On the left are digital public goods: reusable components such as open-source software, open standards, open data, open content and, in some cases, open AI models. On the right are digital public infrastructure layers: digital identity, payments, data exchange and messaging systems used across many public services. Arrows from some left-side items to the right-side items show that digital public goods can be used to build or improve digital public infrastructure. A note at the bottom says the two terms overlap in practice but are not the same: reusable tools are not identical to public service infrastructure, and good governance is still required.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side comparison with fixed arrows from reusable components on the left to infrastructure layers on the right, plus a text note explaining that AI may appear in either column or neither.

workedExample.scenario: A ministry wants to reduce delays in a school meal support programme for low-income households.
workedExample.input: The programme currently uses paper forms, separate district databases and manual payment lists. A team considers adopting an open-source case-management tool and an open standard for secure data exchange.
process: The team identifies the service foundations it needs: identity verification, payment transfer and a data exchange layer between schools and social protection offices.
The open-source case-management tool and the open data standard are treated as reusable components that can be adapted locally.
Developers connect the schools' attendance system to the social protection database through the data exchange layer, with agreed fields and access controls.
Once verified, approved households are added to the payment system, reducing duplicate entry and missed records.
workedExample.result: Processing time falls from 12 days to 4 days in a pilot district. In this example, the payment and data exchange layers are part of DPI, while the open-source tool and open standard are DPG-style components that helped implement it.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN country team is reviewing options to support a government-led household assessment system and wants to understand whether proposed digital tools are core public-service infrastructure or reusable public digital components.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The distinction helps staff discuss procurement, interoperability, capacity-building and governance more clearly. It also helps them avoid treating every open digital tool as infrastructure, or every infrastructure project as automatically open and reusable.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload personal, household-level, protection-sensitive or confidential assessment data into an unapproved public AI service or unvetted public platform while exploring DPI or DPG options. Use approved systems, data protection safeguards and human oversight.

whyItMatters: These terms matter because they shape real choices about how digital services are built, funded and governed. If people mix them up, they may buy a single app when they really need shared infrastructure, or they may assume that using open tools automatically solves questions about privacy, accountability, inclusion or sustainability. For policy and programme staff, the distinction helps in conversations about procurement, standards, long-term maintenance, vendor dependence, national ownership and cross-border cooperation. It also matters in AI discussions, because AI tools may be added to public digital systems, but the public-interest questions remain broader than the model itself.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: DPI and DPG are just two names for the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are closely related but not identical. DPI usually refers to the shared digital systems that many public services depend on. DPG usually refers to reusable digital resources, often openly licensed or openly governed, that can help build or improve those systems.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If software is open source, it automatically counts as a digital public good.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Open source is important, but it is not the whole test. In many policy discussions, a digital public good is expected to show public benefit, usable documentation, and attention to issues such as privacy, inclusion or harm reduction. Different organisations may apply somewhat different criteria.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Building DPI is mainly a technical project.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Technical design matters, but public infrastructure also depends on law, governance, financing, accountability, accessibility, cybersecurity and human rights protections. A technically strong system can still fail the public if these parts are weak.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Think of DPI as the shared digital foundations that many public services use, and DPGs as reusable digital parts that can help build those foundations.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Digital public infrastructure commonly refers to foundational, population-scale or economy-wide digital systems that support multiple public or public-interest services, such as identity, payments, registries, consent or data exchange mechanisms. Digital public goods commonly refers to reusable digital assets, often including open-source software, open standards, open data, open content and sometimes open AI models, that are intended for broad public benefit and reuse. The relationship is functional, not identical: DPGs can be inputs into DPI, but DPI also depends on institutional arrangements, legal authority, governance, financing, operations, security controls and lifecycle management. The exact boundary of what qualifies as a DPG is not fully settled across all actors, so it is better to state the criteria being used rather than assume universal agreement.

keyTakeaway: DPI is the shared digital foundation for services; DPGs are reusable digital components that may help build that foundation, but the two terms are not interchangeable.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between digital public infrastructure and digital public goods?
options: They are exact synonyms for any government technology project.
DPI is the shared service foundation, while DPGs are reusable digital components that can help build or improve it.
DPGs are only about AI models, while DPI is only about broadband cables.
If a system is used by the public, it is automatically both DPI and a DPG.
quickCheck.explanation: The key distinction is role. DPI refers to foundational digital systems used across services, such as identity or payments. DPGs refers to reusable digital resources, such as open-source software or standards, that may support those systems. Public use alone does not make something both.

contested: The broad idea is widely used, but the exact criteria for what should count as a digital public good, and sometimes the scope of digital public infrastructure, are not fully settled across all organisations and policy forums.

issues.problem: This merges the two terms into one vague description instead of assigning a distinct meaning to each. A reader cannot tell which phrase defines DPI and which defines DPGs.
issues.fix: DPI provides shared digital systems across services; DPGs are open, reusable resources that may help build them for public benefit.

issues.problem: The page weakens openness from a defining feature into something that is merely usual. Saying DPGs are "often openly licensed or openly governed" suggests that open governance can substitute for an open resource. The page also lists open standards as DPGs without distinguishing an open standard from the separate term "international standard."
issues.fix: Open source is important, but it is not the whole test. A digital public good must fall within an open category, such as open-source software, open data or open standards, and meet public-interest criteria on matters such as privacy, inclusion and harm reduction. The criteria used should be stated.

issues.problem: The input proposes an "open standard for secure data exchange," but the process changes this to an "open data standard." Those are not equivalent. In a household assessment context, the latter can also be misread as making protected household data open.
issues.fix: The open-source case-management tool and the open standard are treated as reusable components that can be adapted locally.

issues.problem: Option 1 is the only defensible answer, but the quiz is too easy to test understanding. Option 0 is false because the terms are not synonyms and do not cover every government project. Option 1 correctly distinguishes infrastructure from reusable resources. Option 2 is an absurd restriction to AI models and broadband cables. Option 3 is false because public use does not determine either classification. The three distractors can be rejected from their absolute wording and caricatures alone.
issues.fix: Use these options: ["DPI and DPG both require every component to be open.", "DPI is the shared service foundation, while DPGs are reusable digital components that can help build or improve it.", "DPGs are the governance rules for DPI, while DPI is its software.", "Any openly licensed component used in DPI is automatically a DPG."]

issues.problem: The explanation only addresses the original public-use distractor. It would not explain why the more plausible revised alternatives are wrong.
issues.fix: Option 1 is the only correct statement. DPI can use closed or open components, so it does not require every component to be open. DPGs are reusable resources, not DPI governance rules. An open licence alone does not establish that a resource meets the other DPG criteria.
